union-intersection.desc: Union (A | B): the value can be either type. Intersection (A & B): the value must satisfy both types simultaneously.
union-intersection.qsub: Draw the mental Venn diagram. Why does an intersection of {a:string} & {a:number} produce {a:never} instead of a valid type?
union-intersection.what:
| and & seem opposite, and that's the most common confusion.

A | B = value can be A or B. Therefore you can only use what is present in both — fewer properties.
A & B = value has fields of A and B. More properties.
union-intersection.analogy: Union = "tea or coffee" — not sure which, so you can only ask for what both have (is it hot?). Intersection = "coffee with tea" — both qualities together.
union-intersection.why: Union is the thing TypeScript uses to model "these three states can occur" — loading / success / error, or different event types. And together with narrowing (next topic) is the way you safely handle those states.
pros: Impossible states cannot be written.
Merging props with Intersection is a one-line job.
The compiler forces handling every case (exhaustive check).
cons: You have to narrow before using anything from a Union.
Error messages for large unions become very long.
| and & seem opposite.
gotchas: Union gives fewer properties, Intersection gives more — it feels opposite but is correct upon reflection.
The intersection of two primitives is never — no value can be both.
Include a common literal field in Union members (e.g., status) — that makes narrowing much easier.
terms: "Either this or that" — one of the two.
Reaching a single type from a Union by applying checks.
where: loading / success / error — three different shapes, one type.
Different shapes for success and failure.
union-intersection.visualCap: In a Union the value is of a single type (but unknown which), so only common properties are available. In an Intersection both sets of fields are present together.

type-vs-interface.qsub: Can a type extend an interface? Can an interface extend a type? Show both syntaxes and explain the subtle differences in behaviour.
type-vs-interface.what:
In 90% of cases they behave the same. There are two real differences:

1. type can be given any name — union, primitive, tuple. interface only describes an object shape.
2. When you write interface again with the same name it merges. type gives an error.
type-vs-interface.why: The same merging that is a feature for library authors (you can add your field to third-party types) becomes a bug in your own code — you wrote the same name in two places and didn’t notice.
pros: interface error messages are a bit clearer.
type can name anything.
Merging lets you extend third-party types.
cons: Accidental merging happens silently — no warning.
Choosing between them confuses newcomers for no reason.
type error messages become very long for large unions.
gotchas: Interview answer: "type can be given any name; interface only merges on object shapes." Everything else is detail.
Accidental merging is a real bug — if you write interface Config in two places they will silently merge.
interface can extend a type and vice-versa — they work together.
terms: Object blueprint. Merges when declared again.
Naming any type — union, primitive, function, object.
Interfaces with the same name automatically combine.
where: Both work. Choose one within the team and stick to it.

ts-primitives.desc: TypeScript infers types automatically from values. The type system is structural. Const infers literal types; let infers widened types.
ts-primitives.q: What is the difference between type inference and explicit annotation? When does TypeScript infer the wrong type and you must annotate explicitly?
ts-primitives.qsub: What is the difference between let x = 5 (inferred as number) and const x = 5 (inferred as literal 5)? Why does that matter for unions?
ts-primitives.what:
TypeScript mostly recognizes types on its own. When you write const x = 5 it knows this is a number — you don’t need to write : number.

But there’s a small difference: with const the type is exactly that value, while with let the type becomes wider.
ts-primitives.why: Writing a type everywhere is not the goal of TypeScript. The less you write, the cleaner the code. Write a type where it serves as a contract — function arguments, return type, and exported items. Leave internal variables to inference.
pros: You write less — inference does most of the work.
Specifying a return type catches errors inside the function.
Using as const makes config objects type-safe.
cons: The widening of let can be confusing at first.
Inference sometimes gives a very wide type (e.g., any[]).
Too many annotations make the code noisy.

You should write a function’s return type. Without it, errors surface at the caller rather than inside the function.
The type of const arr = [] becomes never[] — write const arr: string[] = [] instead.

With let the type widens — e.g., "hi" becomes string.

A type that allows only a single value. It seems useless on its own, but with a union it becomes TypeScript's most useful feature.

literal-types.why: With a plain string a typo is not caught — "smal" is also a valid string. With a literal union that mistake is caught while writing, not at runtime.

TypeScript reads your if. Inside if (typeof x === "string") it knows that x is a string — you can write x.toUpperCase().

This is called control flow analysis, and it is the smartest part of TypeScript.

nullability.desc: With strictNullChecks on, null and undefined are their own distinct types — you must explicitly handle them. The non-null assertion (!) removes them unsafely.
nullability.q: What changes when you enable strictNullChecks? Explain the non-null assertion operator (!) and when it is a code smell vs genuinely necessary.
nullability.qsub: What is the difference between optional property a?: string (string | undefined) and a: string | null? When does it matter?
nullability.what:
Without strictNullChecks, null hides in every type — string means "string or null", and TypeScript can't protect you.

With it, null and undefined become separate types, and you cannot move forward without handling them.
nullability.why: "Cannot read properties of undefined" is the most common JavaScript crash. strictNullChecks catches that entire class of bugs before they run with a single flag. It is the most beneficial TypeScript flag — therefore strict: true should always be on.
pros: The most common JavaScript crash is caught before it runs.
Handling with ?. and ?? stays concise.

When migrating an old project, enable it file-by-file rather than all at once.

enums.desc: Regular enums generate a runtime JS object. const enums are erased at compile time (inlined). String literal unions are the modern, zero-runtime alternative.
enums.q: What is the difference between a regular enum, const enum, and a string literal union? Why do many teams prefer union types over enums?
enums.qsub: What is the enum isolation problem with const enum across module boundaries? Why does isolatedModules forbid const enums from external modules?
enums.what:
enum seems like a natural feature of TypeScript — but it is one of the few things that generates real JavaScript code at runtime. The rest of the type system disappears after compilation; there is no enum.

And in most cases a simple literal union does the job better.
enums.why:
Enums have three hidden drawbacks: they add extra code to the bundle, numeric enums are not type-safe (any number can be used), and they are TypeScript-only — they behave oddly when imported from plain JavaScript.

Therefore today’s advice: use the default union, and use an enum only when you truly need reverse mapping.

String enums appear clear during debugging.
Reverse mapping (number → name) is provided only by enums.
cons: Numeric enums are not type-safe — any number can be used.
Adds real code to the bundle — union has zero cost.
const enum breaks with modern bundlers (Vite/esbuild).
gotchas: In a numeric enum, let s: Size = 99 passes. If you must use an enum, choose a string enum.
const enum breaks with isolatedModules — if you’re using Vite/esbuild, don’t use it at all.
Interview answer: "default union, because zero runtime cost and full type safety; enums only for reverse mapping."

Same, but values are inlined at compile time.
"a" | "b" — often a better alternative to enums.
where: Literal union — should be the default.
When you need a name from a number — then use an enum.
Enums will be present — no need to change them, just use unions in new code.

structural-typing.what: TypeScript does not look at the name of a type — it looks at whether its shape matches. If an object has the required fields, it will be considered that type, even if it has never heard the interface's name.
structural-typing.analogy: Duck typing: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, then it is a duck." The name doesn't matter; it's about behavior.
structural-typing.why: Because of this, you can pass third-party objects to your functions without modifying them. But there is a drawback: UserId and PostId are both string, so TypeScript treats them as the same thing — and passing the wrong id is not caught. (The remedy is “branded types.”)
pros: Flexible — objects don’t need to implement an interface.
Works easily with third-party code.
Creating mock objects for testing is very easy.
cons: Different things with the same shape become interchangeable (UserId vs PostId).
The rules of excess property checking seem odd at first.
You have to improvise (branding) for nominal typing.
gotchas: Excess property check applies only to object literals. It doesn’t apply when assigning from a variable — that’s the behavior that confuses people.
Structural typing means that UserId and PostId (both strings) are the same — real ID mix-up bugs arise from this.

keyof-typeof.desc: keyof T yields a union of known public property names of T. typeof gives you the type of a value at the type level — essential for extracting types from values.
keyof-typeof.what:
Two small operators that together form the most commonly used TypeScript pattern.

keyof T = union of all keys of T. typeof x = type of the value x. Combined: "give the type of this object's keys".
keyof-typeof.why: Without it you have to write keys manually — and the day you add a new key to the object, the type stays old and the mistake goes unnoticed. With keyof typeof the type always stays in sync with the object.
pros: The type stays always in sync with the object.
No need to write keys manually.
The return type of generic functions becomes exact.

keyof also brings in optional and readonly keys.

indexed-access.desc: T[K] accesses the type at key K within T. Supports nested access, union keys, and extends keyof constraints. Enables type-safe property lookups.
indexed-access.qsub: What happens when K is not a valid key of T? How do you constrain K at the type level? What is the difference between T[string] and T[keyof T]?
indexed-access.what:
Just as you extract a value with user.name, you can extract a type with User["name"].

And for arrays, T[number] — “what’s inside this array.”
indexed-access.why: Re-writing a type is the most common source of bugs — the original changes, but the copy stays old. With indexed access you extract a type, you don’t write it. Whatever changes, it updates automatically.
pros: Type duplication eliminated completely.
When the original changes, the extracted type updates automatically.

ts-decorator-composition.q: How do decorators compose? What is the execution order when you apply multiple decorators to a single method?
ts-decorator-composition.qsub: How does NestJS use decorators for route definition? What is the difference between @Controller and @Injectable decorators?
ts-decorator-composition.what:
Definition: Applying multiple decorators to a method/class. There are two different orders and this is a favorite interview question:

  • Apply order — bottom-up (bottom-up). The lowest one wraps first.
  • Execution order — at call time top-down. The topmost one is the outermost layer.

Factories are different: in @log(1) @log(2) the factory calls happen top-down, then apply bottom-up.
ts-decorator-composition.analogy: Onion layers. When peeling (apply) it goes from inside to outside; when cutting (call) the outer layer is encountered first.
ts-decorator-composition.why: If you get the order wrong, the bug may not be caught: with @cache @auth cache runs first — meaning an unauthorized user could receive a cached result! @auth @cache is correct — auth check first, then cache.
pros: Create small, focused decorators and combine them
Each concern lives in its own layer — clean separation
Changing the order changes behavior
cons: The order bug is completely silent
After 3+ layers debugging becomes painful
Each layer appears as a frame in the stack trace
gotchas: Apply bottom-up, execution top-down — they are reversed, and that's what interviewers ask
Always place @auth above @cache, otherwise a cached response could be sent without auth
Factory calls (the ones with arguments) happen first, top-to-bottom — a third distinct order

the lowest decorator is applied first
